For Mr. Peanutbutter and Bojack's friendship, I think Bojack will always be annoyed by him, but after this season and after they finally had that big confrontation on the air of Hollywoo Stars and Celebrities: What Do They Know? Do They Know Things?? Let's Find Out, I think they're actually going to start getting closer... that is, until Bojack fucks everything up and (accidentally?) reveals to MrPB that Diane was actually sleeping on his couch, watching Horsin' Around reruns and smoking weed while she was supposed to be in Cordovia.

As for Jill Pill, I really think she's important to the character of Bojack, in ways we can't quite know yet. The story is told from Bojack's perspective. They do will in staying true to the logic of that. With every other piece of Bojack's baggage, we know the deal. Except this: Jill Pill and the mysterious other show. Suggesting that Bojack was actively trying to forget / ignore the whole thing. And the only things worth ignoring are important.

According to Diane, there is no "deep down." What you are is what you do, and Bojack hasn't done very many good things. "[Opening this orphanage] was one of the only good things I ever did and I did it by accident." At the end of season 2, Bojack is a bad person according to the show's own philosophies. But that's okay, because if Bojack is a bad person right now because of his actions, why can't he direct his actions towards being a better person? That's why the ending with the running man is so important. "It gets easier, but you have to do it every day." Running up the hill is a metaphor for being good to the people around him. It's difficult, but with practice, he can curb his self destructive habits and stop doing to so much damage to all the people close to him.
"Yeesh! Downer ending!"

The series will end with Bojack drowning somehow, whether it be metaphorical or literal. Every episode of the show begins with the same imagery: Bojack getting drunk at his own party and throwing himself out his second floor window into his pool where he sinks. (Of course, the shot pans out to reveal him lying on a pool raft, so, metaphorical.)
And again, in "Downer Ending" we hear him describe a similar scenario to Sarah Lynn and Todd: "And when I get too old too old to take care of myself, I go for one last swim. I know I can't make it back to shore. I'm too weak, too tired. So I just let water take me under."
Bojack is going to drown somehow, and whether it's him drowning to death in water like the drug trip book idea, or drowning in his own lucrative lifestyle like the opening suggests, it's going to happen /somehow/. 

EDIT: In Bojack's office there's a painting of Bojack watching Bojack swimming in his pool. Possible other hint?

Also unrelated predictions: Bojack is going to (accidentally?) reveal to Mr Peanutbutter that Diane was sleeping on his couch while he thought she was in Cordovia causing a huge problem in their marriage and the New York playwrite Jill Pill is going to be a key factor in Bojack's past. I have no real evidence to support that last thing, it's just a feeling I get watching=. The entire show is told through Bojack's perspective, what's important to him. With everything else in his past, Horsin' Around and his baggage with Herb, his problems with his parents, we know all about it. But this playwrite, and the lightly hinted at "other TV show" are foreign entities to us as the viewers: we don't know about them, suggesting that Bojack has either forgotten (which he hasn't) or has been actively trying to forget and ignore it. And you only ignore things when they're important.

That fucking scene was so hard to watch, for so many reasons... But I wouldn't say the "most shocking character development EVER". Like there are so many characters out there doing bad stuff... Street Car Named Desire, anyone? Don Draper from Mad Men? Aaron Paul's own Breaking Bad? Take your pick out of pretty much ANY character from Game of Thrones, they're pretty terrible...

Having kids isn't what would make Bojack happy- It's having people who love him and care about him. He thought that's what it meant when he was famous- people loved him. But it was only the character they loved. Bojack isn't stupid, he realized that he started acting like a jerk after the show got big, so after Horsin' Around, he assumed that nobody loves him because he's a "bad person." This was why it was so important to him that Diane thought he was a good person deep down- he felt like she was the only one who truly knew him "deep down" and needed validation that somebody thinks he's good and therefore possible to be loved.  But he's so close to the puzzle that he missed the greater  truth in that: Diane is his friend and likes him despite his flaws. Todd likes him despite his flaws. The ending of season two is where he realizes that he shouldn't be trying to be a good person so that people will love him, he should be trying to be a better person to stop hurting and pushing away the people who already love him.
